title: The Blacksmith Who Ignited Korea's Alphabet
event_summary: Royal metalworker Jang Yeong-sil and a team of craftsmen at the Jiphyeonjeon (Hall of Worthies) perfected the movable copper type matrices needed to mass-produce King Sejong's newly invented Hangul alphabet. While Sejong designed the script's radical phonetic logic, it was Jang's innovations in precision metal casting — building on his earlier breakthroughs in astronomical instruments — that made it physically possible to print and distribute the Hunminjeongeum, the document promulgating the new writing system. Without a viable printing technology matched to the script's geometric letterforms, Hangul would have remained a palace curiosity instead of reaching the literate classes.
why_forgotten: Confucian elites who controlled Korean historiography actively opposed Hangul, calling it 'vulgar script' and lobbying to suppress it for centuries in favor of Classical Chinese. Jang Yeong-sil himself was eventually disgraced over an unrelated incident involving a broken royal palanquin and stripped from official records. The technical achievement of adapting movable type to a brand-new alphabet was overshadowed by the narrative of Sejong as a lone genius-king.
why_it_matters: Hangul is now considered one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created, and South Korea's near-perfect literacy rate — among the highest on Earth — traces directly to its accessibility. The metallurgical techniques Jang pioneered influenced East Asian printing for centuries and prefigured industrial standardization. Today, Hangul's elegant logic has made it a model for linguists designing writing systems for previously unwritten languages across Southeast Asia and Africa.
